story: For 30 years after Nelson Mandela's election in 1994, the African National Congress governed South Africa on its own. In 2024, worn down by corruption, power cuts and unemployment above 30 percent, it lost its majority for the first time, and Cyril Ramaphosa formed a Government of National Unity with its old rival, the business-friendly Democratic Alliance, the party many black South Africans long saw as representing white interests (Friedrich Naumann Foundation). Against expectations, the coalition has mostly held. In 2026 it faces its first big test at the ballot box.

Municipal elections are on 4 November, and they matter more than usual because South Africa's cities are where government visibly fails: water cuts, collapsing roads and uncollected rubbish. The DA chose a new leader, Geordin Hill-Lewis, the mayor of Cape Town, in April, and is running former party leader Helen Zille for mayor of Johannesburg, the economic hub (Financial Mail). One poll in Tshwane, home to the capital Pretoria, had the DA on 43 percent and the ANC on 32. The ANC is squeezed from all sides: its ally the Communist Party is running separately in protest at the coalition, and Jacob Zuma's MK party and the EFF compete for its base (EWN). Analysts expect a record number of hung councils. Meanwhile, the ANC is quietly fighting over who succeeds Ramaphosa, and tensions with the Trump administration weigh on trade.
briefing.power: A parliamentary republic. The 400-member National Assembly, elected by proportional representation, elects the president, who is both head of state and government, for up to two five-year terms. The nine provinces and the municipalities have their own elected governments.
briefing.holders: President Cyril Ramaphosa (ANC), leading the Government of National Unity since 2024.
